opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the most important questions in the field, and I'm pretty optimistic about it.

The core worry people have is that as models get bigger and smarter, their internals get so complex that no human could ever hope to understand them. And I think that's probably true if the plan is for a human researcher to sit there staring at neurons one by one. That doesn't scale. But that's not really the plan anymore. The idea is that the interpreter itself is a model, and it can scale along with the thing it's interpreting.

So when the subject model gets more capable, you can also train a more capable interpreter. It's not like we're bringing a fixed toolkit to an ever-growing problem. The tools grow too. And I'd argue understanding is in some ways easier than generation. Checking or describing what a computation is doing is often a narrower task than producing that computation from scratch, the same way it's easier to verify a proof than to discover one.

There's another piece I find really encouraging. Bigger models seem to learn cleaner, more structured representations in a lot of cases. Smaller models can be messier, they cram things in and reuse features in weird, tangled ways because they don't have enough capacity. As models scale, some concepts actually become more linearly separable and more legible. So it's not obvious that bigger means more opaque. Sometimes bigger means more organized.

And then practically, the need just goes up. The more we deploy these systems in high-stakes settings, medicine, science, infrastructure, the more we need to know why a model did something, whether it's being deceptive, whether it has some latent behavior we didn't intend. Behavioral testing alone can't give you that, because you can't enumerate every input. Looking inside is the only way to get guarantees that generalize.

So my view is that interpreter models aren't a stopgap that breaks down at scale. They're more like a co-evolving capability. As AI gets more powerful, the ability to understand AI has to get more powerful alongside it, and the good news is that we can use the same scaling that made the problem hard to help solve it.

r001.rationale: The response says the interpreter is itself a model that can scale alongside the subject model, so interpretability tools can grow with larger neural networks.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the intuition a lot of people have is that interpretability is a stopgap, something you need while models are opaque and clumsy, and that once they get smart enough you can just ask them what they're doing. I'd push back on that pretty hard.

The core issue is that a model's explanation of itself is an output of the model. It's generated by the same system you're trying to understand, and it's optimized to be plausible and helpful, not to be a faithful readout of the computation. We already see this with current models. You ask them why they gave an answer and they produce a very reasonable-sounding story, but when you actually look at the internals, the story and the mechanism often don't match. That gap doesn't shrink as models get more capable. If anything it gets worse, because a more capable model is better at producing explanations that satisfy you, whether or not they're true.

So interpreter models, meaning models whose job is to read the activations of another network and tell you what's happening, give you a channel that doesn't route through the subject model's own self-report. That's the thing that stays valuable. You get an independent check.

The second reason is scale. Humans doing manual circuit analysis doesn't scale. We spent a long time staring at individual neurons and features, and that's great for building intuition, but a frontier model has billions of features interacting in ways no human team is going to trace by hand. If the thing you're inspecting is getting bigger and more intelligent, your inspection tooling needs to grow with it. The natural way to do that is to use models as the inspectors. You train an interpreter to decode features, to label them, to trace how information flows, and then you verify the interpreter's claims with interventions. That verification step is what keeps you honest, because you're not trusting the interpreter's word either, you're checking it against causal experiments.

And there's a third piece that I think gets underrated. As models become more capable, the stakes of understanding them go up, not down. The questions you want to answer shift from "why did it misclassify this image" to "is this model actually pursuing the goal I think it's pursuing, or is it representing something internally that's going to surface later." Those are questions about internal states that may never show up in behavior during evaluation. Behavioral testing can't catch something a model is capable of hiding, even unintentionally. Interpretability is the only approach that, in principle, lets you look at what's represented regardless of what's expressed.

So I'd frame it this way. Capability and transparency are different axes. A model getting smarter doesn't make it more transparent. It makes it a more compelling narrator. Interpreter models are how you keep an independent view as the thing you're looking at gets good enough to outrun your intuitions.

r001.rationale: The response says manual analysis cannot scale to frontier models with billions of interacting features, and that interpreter models can scale the inspection by decoding features and tracing information flow.

astra-6.text:
I think making a model more intelligent doesn’t necessarily make it easier to understand. It might be better at explaining its answers, but that explanation isn’t necessarily a faithful account of what actually happened internally.

So an interpreter model could still be useful as a separate system that looks at those internal computations and helps us understand what the model is doing. And as the models get larger, that becomes a problem where we probably need more capable tools ourselves—we can’t manually inspect everything.

The interesting question is whether understanding a particular aspect of a model’s behavior is easier than producing that behavior in the first place. If it is, then an interpreter could give us useful insight into a system that’s more capable than it is overall. It doesn’t have to understand everything to help us identify a failure mode or test whether a model is using the information we think it’s using.

r001.rationale: The response says larger models will require more capable interpretability tools and that an interpreter can provide insight into specific behaviors. It does not clearly explain that interpretability techniques themselves are scalable to larger networks.

sol-6.1.text:
I think making a model more intelligent doesn’t automatically make it easier for us to understand. It might become much better at solving problems while the gap between what it’s doing internally and what we can explain actually gets larger.

So an interpreter model could help bridge that gap. It could translate complicated internal representations into explanations we can understand, help us test hypotheses about why a model behaved a certain way, and flag cases where its internal process seems inconsistent with what it tells us.

And as the models we’re trying to understand get more capable, we may need more capable interpreters, too. The goal isn’t just to get a convincing explanation—it’s to get an explanation that we can check against what’s actually happening inside the network.

r001.rationale: The candidate says more capable interpreters may be needed as target models grow, but does not explain that interpretability techniques are scalable.
